baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Recasts reserve agriculture as a history of Indigenous initiatives and government constraints rather than an assumed cultural rejection of farming (Lost Harvests, 1990).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary preface ix–x, read in the reprint marked 2000, retaining the 1990 publication. Carter describes a change in her own initial hypothesis after examining sources; her claim concerns many, not all, reserve residents. This arrow records her historical interpretation, not independent verification of the unread chapters. Collective regional/encounter comparisons edge_809 and edge_869 retain their original IDs and endpoints.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Joins racial imagery and the regulation of marriage to the history of women’s unequal options and colonial nation-building in the Prairie West (1997; 2008).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Capturing Women, complete preface xiii–xvi, and The Importance of Being Monogamous, opening pp. 3–9, read. These are different investigations: constrained public representations and the imposition/contestation of marital norms. The latter also states limits to state power and the persistence of Indigenous marriage law. The arrow does not substitute the publisher summary for a whole-book reading or give one experience to all women.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Examines how British women’s struggles for prairie land combined gendered exclusion with unequal participation in Indigenous dispossession (Imperial Plots, 2016; read in corrected reprint 2018).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Read introduction pp. 3–11, 19–23. P. 6 explicitly engages Wolfe, while pp. 9–10 qualify settler women’s privileges and complicity; the later pages explain cross-border and imperial scales. The source now exceeds the prior publisher-page-only evidence, whose wording and date remain in its verification history. This contribution concerns this specific later work; it neither assigns her entire earlier bibliography to one paradigm nor asserts an influence relationship from the citation alone.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Carter’s appreciative review of On the Edge of Empire asks for fuller North American comparison and more evidence of Indigenous social centrality, political agency and initiatives (2002/03).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The signed review praises the gender/race analysis and conclusion while making these two requests on p. 119. It does not say Perry denied Indigenous resistance. The reviewed book is not newly read.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: In her 2003 review, Beatrice Medicine identifies Ahenakew among the Indigenous scholars whose historical insights inform Carter’s 1999 survey.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Explicitly attributed scholarly review of Aboriginal People and Colonizers of Western Canada to 1900; the book body remains unread. This records reported use of historical insight, not mentorship, exclusive influence or a verified particular Ahenakew work. Medicine’s Big Bear example and Christine Welsh’s formulation are not assigned to Ahenakew.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Dickason praises Carter’s corrective history of western Canada but argues that it idealizes Indigenous societies and generalizes equality too broadly (2001).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: A bounded criticism within an appreciative review of Aboriginal People and Colonizers of Western Canada to 1900. The substantive review is reproduced in the institutional repository’s abstract field; that primary text was read, but the PDF returned 403 and was not facsimile-collated. Carter’s book body remains unread. Dickason’s separate buffalo example is not needed to substantiate this relationship.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Medicine’s 2003 review identifies Dickason’s historical insights among the Indigenous scholarly resources Carter uses in her history of Aboriginal people and colonizers in western Canada.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Explicitly attributed to Beatrice Medicine’s substantive review of Carter’s 1999 book, whose body remains unread. Harold Cardinal, Paul Chartrand and Edward Ahenakew retain co-credit. This establishes reported use of historical insight, not mentorship, exclusive influence, or a particular Dickason work. It is distinct from Dickason’s own 2001 criticism of Carter; Medicine’s Big Bear example and Christine Welsh’s formulation are not assigned to Dickason.

(2004, abstract) treat 1710 through its effects on "aboriginal inhabitants, Acadians, and New Englanders" at local, regional and imperial scales; Carter (1990) and Stonechild and Waiser (1997) are western examples (catalogue level). The PhD overlap is the strongest of this entry's Canadian links. PhD context: 153 of 194 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with Canadian regional history also engage the Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history anchor set (79% vs 19% of all; lift 4.21). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Gender and race in the making of a would-be white settler colony: British Columbia, 1849–71, where colonization and immigration were meant to produce a white, respectable society among a majority of Aboriginal people and failed to do so (2001), which she said was inspired by an international literature on gender and colonialism (no derivation from Wolfe's settler-colonial theory is established by the texts checked); later described by her as a comparative settler-colonial argument (2016)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History', BC Studies 132 (2001/02), pp. 57–64, read in full: On the Edge of Empire 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism. That through reading about imperialism elsewhere I came to see imperialism where I was is a suggestive comment on the convenient erasure of dispossession' (p. 58; the sentence ends 'settler consciousness' without a connecting word); 'The most remarkable pattern of silence probably concerns Aboriginal peoples' (p. 61). The 1995 essay (pp. 42–43, read) calls British Columbia 'a racially divided one controlled by a minority white population constantly engaged in a process of colonization' (p. 42). The book is unread; reviewers quote it: 'In contemporary newspapers and conversations, White British Columbians often long for the days when our society was unquestionably British … When we do so we long for a fiction of our own invention' (p. 201, as quoted by Carter, p. 117). In-period reviews. Sarah Carter, BC Studies 136 (2002/03), pp. 117–119, read in full: 'British Columbia fits within a broader context of European colonialism in that it was a settler colony where dispossesion [sic] of the indigenous societies and resettlement by a newcomer population were intertwined. While this is imperial history, it is not an example of the triumph of imperialism as in this era Aboriginal peoples remained demographically dominant and socially central' (p. 117); but 'The theme of the "social centrality and political agency" of the Aboriginal peoples of British Columbia could have been further developed' (p. 119). Myra Rutherdale, Labour/Le Travail 50 (2002), pp. 324–326, read in full: Perry shows 'how colonization and immigration worked in tandem in an attempt to create a White colony, while at the same time deliberately marginalizing the majority of the population, the Aboriginal peoples' (p. 325). Paul Orlowski, Left History 8:1 (2002), pp. 119–122, read in full: 'I found Perry's rendering of First Nations resistance to be lacking throughout much of the work, their portrayal emphasizing passivity rather than agency' (p. 121). Her own caution (1995, p. 43): 'my analysis minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: the 2001 essay cites Said, McClintock, Burton and Chakrabarty, not Wolfe, and the book is unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Perry wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later readings, labelled: in the BC Studies 190 forum (2016) she says the 2001 book 'makes the argument that British Columbia's history is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books' (p. 112); Tony Ballantyne (2016, pp. 104–105) reads Colonial Relations (2015) as 'a salutary reminder of the limitations of work that follows Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini in understanding "settler colonialism" as a fundamentally eliminationist project'.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Gender, race and a settler colony, 1995–2001

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Race in the history of white women and gender in the Canadian West: the 'scarcity model' and 'volcano theory' of gender imbalance traced to colonial promoters (1995), and white masculinity, mixed-race relationships and assisted female migration in colonial British Columbia read as the making of whiteness (2001)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”', BC Studies 105/106 (1995), pp. 27–44, read at pp. 27–33 and 42–43: Canadian historians used 'the "scarcity model" (the notion that women's experience improves commensurately with their scarcity) and the "volcano theory" of male sexuality (the assumption of a fixed quantity of male sexual energy)' (p. 27); 'a quarter-century of inquiry into women's history has produced little on the effect of a skewed demography on women's experience' (p. 28); its 'most clear example' is Jan Noel's 'New France: Les femmes favorisées' (p. 29 n. 4); both models 'are based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race. Practitioners of the "scarcity model" never compute aboriginal women (or, for that matter, men) into their arithmetical evaluation' (p. 30); they are 'integral not only to twentieth century scholarship, but also to colonial discourse itself' (p. 31), descending from Wakefield and the colonial promoters (p. 32); white women's experience 'was never determined by gender alone. British Columbia was a class society' (p. 42); 'While gender imbalance increased white women's opportunities for heterosexual contact, it restricted those economic and social possibilities not contained within the heterosexual nexus' (p. 43). On the Edge of Empire (2001) is unread; Orlowski (p. 119) quotes its aim, 'the importance of race to the social experience of gender in nineteenth-century British Columbia' (p. 8), and 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire' (p. 167, quoted p. 120; Carter, p. 119, uses the same phrase). In-period reception, read in full: Carter (2002): 'This book also makes a valuable Canadian contribution to "Whiteness" studies' (p. 117); Rutherdale (2002): 'At the heart of this imagined community was Whiteness' (p. 325), and the reformers' hope that white women were the 'imperial panacea' (p. 4, as quoted p. 326). Critics: Orlowski (2002) holds that she 'fails to invoke what Roediger calls the "wages of whiteness"', leaving 'a binary racial divide that runs through the entire book but did not run through colonial British Columbia', with Chinese labourers set aside (p. 121), and that her claim that 'class relations are central to social relations' receives little attention (p. 121); Carter (p. 119) asks for the North American setting ('This edge of empire had much in common with California'); Rutherdale's 'small quibble' is that the 'Home' and 'Away' relationship 'could be further probed' (p. 326). Distinct from the Van Kirk packet's edges on fur-trade women: this edge is the post-fur-trade settler colony and the critique of the scarcity model.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Mixed-race relationships not to be explained by white women's absence: Perry's 1995 criticism of fur-trade historians, Van Kirk's 'brilliant account' included, for treating intermarriage as the product of that absence, and her 2001 argument (as Carter reports it) that such relationships were 'not confined to the fur trade' and that 'happy stories' of fur-trade marriages can 'obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism'
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 1995 (BC Studies 105/106, read at p. 30): 'Historians of the fur trade, while concerned with establishing the salience of mixed-race relationships, nonetheless explain their frequency as the product of white women's absence'; n. 8: 'For a brilliant account which ultimately suggests that the existence of mixed-race relationships was the result of white women's absence from the fur trade, see Sylvia Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" … Also see Jennifer S. H. Brown, Strangers in Blood … and Robin Fisher, Contact and Conflict'; n. 11 quotes Van Kirk: 'Had it been possible for fur traders to bring their wives out at an earlier date, it is doubtful whether intermarriage with native women would have been so extensive' (Many Tender Ties, p. 173); the 'volcano theory' 'holds that mixed-race relationships are at worst unfathomable and at best the products of abnormal historical circumstances' (p. 30). Qualifications kept: the criticism is of one explanation, not of the field; she calls Van Kirk's account 'brilliant' (p. 30 n. 8) and 'pioneering' (p. 43), and relies on it for the displacement of Aboriginal women (p. 43). 2001: the book is unread; Carter (BC Studies 136, p. 118, read) reports that 'Perry does not write a history of these relationships, noting the difficulties with available sources, but she does argue that they were not confined to the fur trade and could be found in the city, in the country, and in mining towns', and that she 'stresses the need to look beyond the "happy stories," such as the long marriage of James Douglas and Amelia Connolly, that can "obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism" (62)'. In-period counterpoint: Orlowski (2002, p. 121, read) faults the book because 'the mixed-race couples in colonial B.C. had much to do with building alliances, sometimes between Hudson's Bay Company officers and the daughters of Aboriginal chiefs, a strategy that is not considered at all in the book'. No reply by Van Kirk or Brown was checked. Later reading, labelled: in 2016 (p. 113) she proposes thinking 'seriously about fur-trade colonialism as a distinct and meaningful practice of empire' (Colonial Relations, on the Douglas–Connolly family, is unread). Target: Van Kirk's person entry, since the criticism is of her explanation of intermarriage; her entry cites Perry's 2008 essay on her work only as a later reading.
